# Introduction

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Draft section — scaffolding for the results below.
:::

Reservoirs are a central instrument of drought adaptation, yet their long-run effect on
water security is contested. A socio-hydrological view holds that storage buffers
meteorological drought in the short term but may *increase* vulnerability over time by
inducing demand — encouraging the expansion of irrigated, water-dependent land uses that
raise consumptive water use and sharpen the impact of prolonged dry spells (the "reservoir
effect"). Distinguishing this dynamic from the simple fact that reservoirs are *built where
irrigation demand already exists* requires a counterfactual: how would dammed basins have
behaved under the same drought forcing without the reservoir?

Chile offers a strong testbed. Its 2010-onset megadrought is one of the longest instrumental
dry spells on record, and reservoirs are concentrated in the arid, agriculturally intensive
central basins most exposed to it. That very collinearity — reservoirs sit where it is driest
and where the drought bit hardest — is the central identification threat, and one that
basin-mean greenness or calendar-time comparisons cannot resolve. Here we combine a matched
dammed-versus-undammed design with a forcing-conditioned estimand to ask whether reservoirs
create resilience or merely postpone and concentrate vulnerability.
